correctness.rationale: The positive-degree ideal is nilpotent with field quotient, and J^j is precisely the sum of degrees j through 4 (each exterior basis monomial of degree ≥j splits into j positive-degree factors). A closed line satisfies x²=λx; an invertible x then lies on the unit line, and a nonzero nilpotent x forces λ=0. In odd characteristic homogeneous squaring gives 2a∧b and b∧b in distinct degrees, with a∧c+c∧a=0. Alternating normal form shows b∧b=0 iff the rank of b is ≤2: the nonzero degree-four terms for different pairs of symplectic blocks are independent. For fixed a≠0, ker(a∧−) on bivectors is a∧V, of dimension n−1, and every b there has b∧b=0. Thus s1=q^(h+n−1)(q^n−1)/(q−1), algebraically identical to the stated formula. For a=0 and b≠0 there are (q−1)G bivectors (q−1 per two-plane), giving s2=q^hG. The top two depths are ordinary filtered vector-space line counts. In characteristic two, squaring is additive on the commutative algebra and vanishes on each positive-degree basis monomial, giving all filtered lines. Summing the coefficients gives the two stated totals. Independent signed-tuple multiplication with free higher-degree lifts reproduced both n=4 coefficient lists and totals (32768 and 294152).
residual_risks: Independent replay covers F2 and F3 at n=4, not all prime powers; the field-independent argument establishes the full range.

value.rationale: The degree-four quotient is the first truncation retaining the bivector-square obstruction, so the slice is motivated. The statistic is the full line census by an intrinsic filtration, useful as the one-dimensional baseline for subalgebras of these finite local algebras. The simultaneous odd-characteristic incidence/Grassmann counts distinguish two nontrivial strata which an unrefined square-zero count cannot distinguish. The even case and upper depths serve as contrasting boundary coefficients, not standalone novelty claims.
residual_risks: No downstream result concerning larger subalgebras is established or needed for this value assessment.
